title: Australian History · Episode 1
chapters: Matthew Flinders: the man who named Australia

units.t: Australian History. Episode one.
In this episode: The First Fleet and colonisation, Matthew Flinders: the man who named Australia and The gold rushes.
Part one. The First Fleet and colonisation.
In 1788, eleven ships arrived in Sydney Cove.
For Britain it was a new colony; for the land's Aboriginal owners, it was an invasion.
A continent already home.
When Europeans arrived, Australia was home to hundreds of distinct Aboriginal nations and more than 250 languages, with Torres Strait Islander peoples to the north.
Archaeologists agree people have lived here for more than 50,000 years, and excavations at Madjedbebe in Arnhem Land suggest about 65,000, though that date is still debated.
Aboriginal peoples managed the land with fire, fish traps and trade networks, and lived by complex systems of law, kinship and knowledge.
Dutch sailors had mapped parts of the coast from 1606, and James Cook charted the east coast in 1770, claiming it for Britain despite its people.
Why Britain came.
Britain had shipped around 50,000 convicts to its American colonies until the American Revolution ended that option in the 1770s.
Harsh laws made minor thefts serious crimes, and prisons and hulks overflowed.
In 1786 the government chose Botany Bay as a penal colony.
Strategic interests, such as a Pacific base and timber and flax for the navy, may also have played a part.
Captain Arthur Phillip became first governor.
The First Fleet left Portsmouth on 13 May 1787 with eleven ships and roughly 1,400 people, about 750 of them convicts.
It called at Tenerife, Rio de Janeiro and Cape Town.
Botany Bay proved unsuitable, so Phillip moved to Port Jackson, and on 26 January 1788 raised the British flag at Sydney Cove.
Hunger, then growth.
Few convicts had farming skills.
Crops failed in poor, sandy soils, cattle strayed, and supplies were delayed; the store ship Guardian never arrived after hitting an iceberg in 1789.
Rations were cut severely.
The Second Fleet arrived in 1790 with hundreds of convicts dead or dying from neglect.
A smallpox epidemic in 1789 devastated Aboriginal communities around Sydney.
Only in the mid-1790s did Hawkesbury River farms ease food shortages.
About 162,000 convicts were transported to Australia between 1788 and 1868.
Well-behaved convicts could earn a 'ticket of leave', and many emancipists became farmers, merchants and builders.
Governor Lachlan Macquarie, 1810 to 1821, championed them.
Free settlers arrived in growing numbers from the 1820s, and many Australians today have convict ancestors.
Encounters and conflict.
Relations with the Eora began with some curiosity but deteriorated as colonists took fish, land and water.
Hoping to learn the language, Phillip had Aboriginal men captured, including Arabanoo and, later, Bennelong.
Bennelong escaped, then chose to return, and sailed to England with Phillip in 1792.
In 1790 Phillip was speared at Manly but did not retaliate.
Britain treated the land as terra nullius in practice and made no treaties.
As colonists took land for farming and grazing, Aboriginal people resisted, and frontier conflict continued for over a century.
Pemulwuy led resistance around Sydney until he was killed in 1802.
Massacres occurred across the country; after Myall Creek in 1838, seven colonists were hanged, a rare punishment.
Disease, violence and loss of land caused catastrophic population decline.
Remembering 26 January.
The anniversary of the First Fleet's landing gradually became a national holiday, observed on 26 January by all states and territories only from 1994.
For many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, it marks the beginning of dispossession.

On 26 January 1938, the 150th anniversary, Aboriginal activists including William Cooper, Jack Patten and William Ferguson held a Day of Mourning in Sydney, and the date has been a day of protest ever since.
Today Australians hold a range of views: some celebrate, some mourn, some want the date changed.
Understanding these perspectives is part of understanding Australian history.
The key idea: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples had lived in Australia for more than 50,000 years before Europeans arrived.
Part two. Matthew Flinders: the man who named Australia.
He sailed all the way around the continent, was locked up for six and a half years, and published his great work the day before he died.
Then his grave was lost under a railway station.
Tasmania is an island.
Matthew Flinders, born in 1774 in Lincolnshire, said Robinson Crusoe made him want to go to sea.
He joined the Royal Navy at fifteen and sharpened his navigation and chart making under William Bligh on Bligh's second breadfruit voyage.
In 1795 he reached the young colony of New South Wales and befriended the ship's surgeon George Bass, who shared his appetite for exploring the coast in tiny boats.
Europeans had long wondered whether Van Diemen's Land, Tasmania, joined the mainland.
In 1798 and 1799 Flinders and Bass sailed the sloop Norfolk all the way around it, settling the question.
The passage became Bass Strait, at Flinders' suggestion, giving ships from Britain a shorter if stormy route to Sydney.
Around the continent.
Flinders persuaded Sir Joseph Banks and the Admiralty to back a survey of the continent's coastline.
He sailed in 1801 in HMS Investigator with scientists and artists, including botanist Robert Brown and botanical artist Ferdinand Bauer.
He charted the south coast, then the east, rounding Cape York into the Gulf of Carpentaria.
The ship was rotting so badly that he cut the survey short.
He reached Sydney in June 1803, completing the first known voyage all the way around Australia.
Bungaree, a Kuring-gai man from the Broken Bay area, sailed with him and helped communicate with Aboriginal groups.
He is regarded as the first Australian-born person to circumnavigate the continent.
So did Trim, Flinders' clever black cat with white paws, who has statues near Flinders' own, including outside the State Library of NSW.
Shipwreck and prison.
In 1803 Flinders set off for England as a passenger aboard HMS Porpoise, which struck a reef off the Queensland coast, now called Wreck Reef.
The survivors camped on a sandbank while Flinders took a ship's cutter, a small open boat, back to Sydney to organise a rescue.
He then continued towards England in the tiny, badly leaking schooner Cumberland, and in December 1803 put in at Mauritius, then a French colony.
Britain and France were at war again, and the governor, Charles Decaen, suspected him of spying.
Flinders was detained for six and a half years, and used the time to work on his charts and journals.
Trim, who had stayed with him, vanished on the island.
Naming Australia.
Released in 1810, Flinders reached England in poor health and spent his last years preparing his account of the voyages.
The continent was known by names including New Holland and Terra Australis, the "southern land".
Flinders preferred a shorter form, Australia, which he found more pleasing to the ear.
He was not the first to use the word, but he was its most influential champion.
His book, A Voyage to Terra Australis, used Australia in its text, though his publishers kept the older name in the title.
Governor Lachlan Macquarie read it and began using Australia in official correspondence from 1817.
The book was published on 18 July 1814.
Flinders died the next day, aged forty.
Lost and found.
Flinders was buried in a London cemetery, but over the following decades the burial ground was cleared and built over during the expansion of Euston railway station.
His exact resting place was lost, and a story grew that he lay beneath one of the platforms.
In 2019, archaeologists excavating for the High Speed 2 rail project found a coffin with a lead breastplate bearing his name, among tens of thousands of burials.
In 2024 his remains were reburied in his home village of Donington, Lincolnshire.
In Australia his name lives on in places such as Flinders Street in Melbourne, the Flinders Ranges and Flinders University.
The key idea: Flinders joined the navy at fifteen and, with George Bass, proved in 1798 and 1799 that Tasmania is an island.
Part three. The gold rushes.
In the 1850s, gold transformed Australia almost overnight, nearly tripling its population and sparking its most famous rebellion.
Gold fever.
In February 1851, Edward Hargraves found gold near Bathurst in New South Wales.
Within months, richer finds followed in the new colony of Victoria, at Ballarat, Bendigo and Mount Alexander.
Shepherds, clerks, sailors and shopkeepers abandoned their jobs, and some ships in Melbourne's harbour were left stranded when their crews deserted.
People poured in from Britain, Ireland, Europe, the United States and China.
Australia's non-Indigenous population grew from about 430,000 in 1851 to over 1.
1 million by 1861.
Gold wealth paid for public buildings, railways and banks, and Melbourne earned the nickname 'Marvellous Melbourne' by the 1880s.
Many newcomers brought ideas about democracy.
Life on the diggings.
Diggers lived in tents and bark huts, using picks, shovels, pans and cradles to wash gold from dirt.
As surface gold ran out, they sank deep shafts, and later companies crushed quartz with machinery.
Supplies were expensive and diseases like dysentery spread.
A few struck it rich, like the 72-kilogram 'Welcome Stranger' nugget found at Moliagul in 1869.
Most found little, and many made their fortunes by selling supplies, food and services to diggers.
By the late 1850s, around 40,000 Chinese people were in Victoria.
Resentment led to violent attacks, like the Buckland River riot in 1857 and the Lambing Flat riots in NSW in 1860–61.
Colonies imposed special taxes on Chinese arrivals, so many ships landed at Robe in South Australia instead.
This hostility fed into the later White Australia policy.
Eureka and its legacy.
Miners paid an expensive monthly licence, 30 shillings at first, whether they found gold or not, and police conducted brutal 'licence hunts'.
Diggers had no vote.
Anger boiled over at Ballarat in 1854 after a hotel keeper was acquitted of killing a miner.
Led by Peter Lalor, miners swore allegiance to the Southern Cross flag and built a rough stockade.
Early on 3 December 1854, soldiers and police attacked; the fight lasted about 15 minutes, and around 30 people died, mostly miners.
Public sympathy swung behind the miners.
Melbourne juries refused to convict 13 men charged with treason.
The licence was replaced with a cheap miner's right that came with a vote, and Victoria introduced the secret ballot in 1856, which became known worldwide as the 'Australian ballot'.
Later rushes.
Gold fever did not end with the 1850s.
Finds at Gympie in 1867 helped rescue Queensland from debt, and the Palmer River rush in the 1870s drew thousands of Chinese miners to Cape York.
In 1892 Arthur Bayley and William Ford found gold at Coolgardie in Western Australia, and in 1893 Paddy Hannan's find at Kalgoorlie started another stampede.
Water was so scarce that engineer C.
Y.
O'Connor designed a pipeline of over 500 kilometres from near Perth, completed in 1903.
The WA rush multiplied that colony's population, and many eastern miners there helped sway it towards joining Federation.
What gold left behind.
The rushes left grand streetscapes in towns like Ballarat, Bendigo and Beechworth, and Sovereign Hill in Ballarat recreates goldfields life for visitors.
They also sped up the dispossession of Aboriginal peoples, such as the Wadawurrung around Ballarat and the Dja Dja Wurrung around Bendigo, whose lands and waterways were overrun and damaged.
Digging and sluicing stripped forests and choked creeks with silt.
Gold remains important: Australia is one of the world's largest gold producers, with much of it mined in Western Australia.
In an old goldfields town, look for the Chinese joss houses, mullock heaps and ornate banks.
The key idea: Gold finds in 1851 triggered rushes that nearly tripled Australia's population and made Melbourne rich.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Which statement about Australia before 1788 is supported by the evidence?
Answer. People had lived here for over 50,000 years.
Question two. What did Flinders and Bass prove in 1798 and 1799?
Answer. Tasmania is an island, separated from the mainland by a strait.
Question three. How did the gold rushes change Australia?
Answer. Population nearly tripled and wealth grew.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
